title: Is Public Sector a Better Place for Moms to Work? Exploring Sector Difference in Child Penalties on Women
authors: Fangda Ding; Yifan Chen
affiliations: Department of Politics and Public Administration The University of Hong Kong Hong Kong SAR China; School of International and Public Affairs The China Institute for Urban Governance The Shanghai Research Center for Innovation and Policy Evaluation Shanghai Jiao Tong University Shanghai China
abstract: ABSTRACT With commonly stabler and more flexible working environment, is public sector a better place for moms to work? Theorizing child penalties from sector difference perspective, we argue that childbirth may cause less gender gaps in unemployment and earnings but greater gender disparities in working time commitments in the public sector since job stability and family‐friendliness may form gender norms that depreciate women's work in the public sector. We test our hypotheses by employing event study designs using data from China Family Panel Studies (2010–2022). We found that women public employees experienced smaller child penalties in unemployment and earnings while greater child penalties in working hours than private counterparts, which can be explained by greater family responsibilities and spousal depreciation of women's jobs after childbirth. This paper advances theories of gender equity in public administration by proposing distinct child penalties in the public sector that challenges conventional beliefs.

title: Using Representation Learning and Website Text to Identify Competitor Networks
authors: Gerard Hoberg; Craig Knoblock; Gordon Phillips; Jay Pujara; Zhiqiang Qiu; Louiqa Raschid
affiliations: University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California 90089; Tuck School of Business, Dartmouth College, Hanover, New Hampshire 03755; University of Maryland at College Park, College Park, Maryland 20742
abstract: This paper introduces a new approach to identify competitors using company websites to map competitive relationships among public and private firms. We apply representation learning techniques to create embeddings of companies based on website content, emphasizing information about industry-specific products and services. By placing all firms, public and private, within the same embedding space, we construct a peer competitor network that supports analysis of company interactions and market evolution. We label this new approach and set of network competitors as the website text-based network industry classification (WTNIC). We evaluate the quality of the network using multiple ground truth datasets and benchmarks and show that it offers a robust alternative for understanding competition at scale. Despite using noisy website data, WTNIC matches or outperforms prior approaches that rely on curated data. We demonstrate the value of WTNIC through a case study examining how competition from China affects the public and private peers of a focal firm, highlighting the importance of placing both public and private companies within the same embedding space. Funding: This work was supported by the National Science Foundation [Grants 1561068 and 1937153], the Tuck School of Business at Dartmouth College, the USC Marshall Institute for Outlier Research in Business (iORB), and the Smith School of Business at the University of Maryland. title: Personalization, Engagement, and Content Quality on Social Media: An Evaluation of Reddit’s News Feed
authors: Alex Moehring
affiliations: Operations, Information and Decisions, The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia Pennsylvania 19104
abstract: Digital platforms increasingly curate their content through personalized algorithmic feeds. Platforms have an incentive to promote content that increases the predicted engagement of each user to lift advertising revenues. This paper studies how ranking content to maximize engagement affects the credibility of news content with which users engage. In addition, I evaluate how the ranking algorithm itself can be designed to promote engagement with high-credibility content. Using data from the Reddit politics community, I exploit a novel discontinuity in the ranking algorithm to identify the causal effect of a post’s rank on the number of comments it receives. I use this discontinuity to identify a model of user comment decisions and estimate the credibility of news content that users engage with under a personalized engagement-maximizing algorithm. The personalized engagement-maximizing algorithm exacerbates differences in the credibility of news content with which users engage. I then evaluate a credibility-aware algorithm that explicitly promotes credible news publishers and find the platform can substantially increase the share of engagement with high-credibility publishers for a small reduction in total engagement. These findings suggest algorithmic interventions can be a useful tool for managers to balance engagement quantity and content quality. This paper was accepted by Hemant Bhargava, information systems. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06298 .

title: Transaction Hazards Through Ideological Filters: How CEO Political Ideology Influences Vertical Integration Decisions
authors: Holly Loncarich; Mirzokhidjon Abdurakhmonov; Madison L. Schnacker
affiliations: Kansas State University; University of Nebraska-Lincoln
abstract: Why do firms facing similar transaction environments adopt different boundary structures? Transaction cost theory (TCT) predicts governance choices based on transaction hazards, but persistent heterogeneity in vertical integration suggests that such efficiency-based explanations are incomplete. We examine whether CEO political ideology is associated with systematic variation in firm boundary decisions. Drawing on research on political ideology and strategic leadership, we argue that ideological orientations shape how executives evaluate and prioritize governance trade-offs. Using a panel of 1,198 U.S. public firms from 2001 to 2020 and a firm fixed-effects design exploiting CEO successions, we find that firms led by more conservative CEOs exhibit higher levels of vertical integration. This relationship weakens when asset specificity is high and when industries are more concentrated but is not amplified by demand volatility. Our findings suggest that firm boundaries reflect not only transaction conditions but also systematic differences in executive decision-making.

title: Impostors in paradise: Toxic inclusion in elite doctoral education
authors: Adél Pásztor
affiliations: Corvinus University of Budapest, Hungary
abstract: Elite universities have expanded access, but the terms of recognition after admission remain stratified. This article develops the concept of toxic inclusion to capture a form of institutional incorporation in which formal admission coexists with situationally negotiated recognition after entry. Drawing on interviews with Eastern European doctoral students at a prestigious transnational European graduate school, the analysis shows how admission does not itself secure legitimacy, but relocates inequality into everyday processes of evaluation, interaction, and self-positioning where the legibility of prior trajectories within transnational evaluative frameworks becomes consequential. The findings identify four mechanisms through which inequality is reconfigured after admission: legitimacy on loan, epistemic silencing, impostor work and the morality of belonging. While not uniformly experienced, these dynamics show how recognition is negotiated across symbolic, epistemic, affective and moral dimensions, reshaping inequality beyond admission.

title: Misidentification, confusion and uncertainty: How working-class youth interpret their class identities
authors: Amit Singh
affiliations: Social Research Institute, University College London, England, UK
abstract: This paper investigates how predominantly white, working-class young people (aged 16–22 years old) in London, Rochdale and Morecambe conceptualise class within their lives. Despite facing poverty,inequality and exclusion, these individuals frequently misidentify their class, not out of defensiveness, but out of confusion and uncertainty because the language of class does not resonate with them, with the majority of respondents failing to identify as working-class in clear terms. This occurs against the backdrop of highly visible, politicised narratives pertaining to a ‘left behind’, exclusively white, working-class who are said to live in places like Rochdale and Morecambe. The research contributes to the understanding of how young people interpret their class identities through demonstrating that class is shaped by local dynamics in the context of class decomposition and demobilisation. Ultimately, this paper argues that a lack of awareness about class as identity, did not mean that these young people did not understand wider experiences of inequality and hardship. Rather, there is a disjuncture between how class is lived and how class identities are claimed.

title: Socio‐Technical Risk‐Informed AI‐Driven Automation Trustworthiness Evaluation (ST‐RATE): Part 1‐Conceptualization
authors: Muhammad Hammad Khalid; Ha Bui; Ahmad Al Rashdan; Zahra Mohaghegh
affiliations: Socio‐Technical Risk Analysis (SoTeRiA) Laboratory Urbana Illinois USA; Department of Nuclear, Plasma, and Radiological Engineering University of Illinois at Urbana‐ Champaign Urbana Illinois USA; Idaho National Laboratory (INL) Idaho Falls Idaho USA
abstract: ABSTRACT The growing integration of artificial intelligence (AI)‐driven technologies into nuclear power plant (NPP) operations and maintenance holds significant potential to enhance safety, operational efficiency, and reliability. However, deploying such AI‐driven automation technologies in high‐consequence settings requires a rigorous, traceable, and risk‐informed evaluation of their trustworthiness. Although researchers across various domains have proposed definitions and metrics for AI‐driven automation trustworthiness, no agreed‐upon formal or quantitative method exists that is suitable for the highly regulated nuclear sector. To address this gap, this paper, the first in a two‐part series, presents three contributions: (I) a cross‐disciplinary literature review that categorizes existing definitions and evaluation methodologies for AI‐driven automation trustworthiness and identifies their inherent limitations with respect to applicability in the nuclear domain; (II) develops a new definition of AI‐driven automation trustworthiness as “the degree of confidence that the AI‐driven automation system will function as expected across its conditions of use” to address the limitations identified in Contribution I; and (III) building on the new definition, conceptualizes the Socio‐Technical Risk‐informed AI‐driven Automation Trustworthiness Evaluation (ST‐RATE) methodology, grounded in three foundational pillars: (a) risk‐informed performance expectations, (b) socio‐technical context across operational conditions, and (c) uncertainty‐based trustworthiness evaluation. While developed primarily for the nuclear domain, the definition and ST‐RATE methodology has the potential to be adapted for other safety‐critical domains with appropriate modifications. The ST‐RATE methodological framework is operationalized and demonstrated through an AI‐driven automated firewatch case study in a companion paper (Companion paper Part 2, 2025). ST‐RATE is the first‐of‐its‐kind methodology that enables risk‐informed and uncertainty‐based quantification of trustworthiness despite limited empirical data and without over‐reliance on subjective expert judgment, addressing the key limitations of existing approaches identified in the literature review.

title: The Distinct Roles of Anger and Hope in PFAS Risk Processing: Integrating Mixed Emotional Appeals and Efficacy Information into the EPPM
authors: Yuan Zhong; Hongjiang Li
affiliations: School of Media and Communication Shanghai Jiao Tong University Shanghai China; College of Journalism, Communication and Publishing Sichuan University Chengdu China
abstract: ABSTRACT Guided by the Extended Parallel Process Model (EPPM), this study examines the distinct persuasive mechanisms of mixed emotional appeals and efficacy information in the context of environmental risk communication (per‐ and polyfluoroalkyl substances, PFAS). Results of a 3 (emotional appeals: fear/fear + anger/fear + hope) × 2 (efficacy information: low/high) between‐subjects experiment ( N = 405) in China revealed that adding anger to fear appeals significantly increased perceived threat, whereas adding hope enhanced perceived self‐efficacy. Although providing high‐efficacy information enhanced perceived efficacy, it led to a minor reduction in perceived threat. Notably, the interaction analyses showed that high‐efficacy information increased response efficacy most strongly in the fear + anger condition. In contrast, fear + hope appeals enhanced self‐efficacy even when efficacy information was low. Furthermore, only perceived threat and response efficacy emerged as significant predictors of preventive behaviors. Theoretical implications for expanding the EPPM to include mixed emotions and practical implications for designing PFAS risk messages are discussed.

title: Interactions Among Three‐Tier Factors of Community Safety Resilience: A Dual‐Perspective Analysis
authors: Lipeng Fu; Yuchen He; Xueqing Wang; Boting Zhao; Heng Zhao
affiliations: School of Economics and Management Fuzhou University Fuzhou P. R. China; College of Management and Economics Tianjin University Tianjin P. R. China; Fujian Early Warning Center Fuzhou P. R. China; School of Management Tianjin University of Technology Tianjin P. R. China
abstract: ABSTRACT Enhancing community safety resilience (CSR) is critical for sustainable urban development. Disregarding the complex interactions among CSR factors may cause imbalanced resilience building, limiting a community's capacity to respond to uncertain disasters. This study aims to identify principal CSR factors and examine their interaction mechanisms in the context of Chinese urban communities. We identified 101 factors spanning government, community, and personal tiers. Their interactions were assessed via expert elicitation and analyzed using directed weighted network theory and a modified susceptible‐infectious‐recovered model. The factor interaction network exhibits a sparse, highly modular, core‐periphery structure with small‐world and scale‐free properties. Community‐level governance and infrastructure, together with personal‐level physiological and psychological factors, serve as both hubs and intermediary bridges. Government‐level top‐level design, organizational leadership, and support and investment act as primary drivers, critical in initiating and mitigating risk propagation. Fundamental risk mitigation, especially under dual perturbations, depends on government action, whereas community‐level factors are vital for localized response. These findings provide an analytical foundation for prioritizing interventions and designing system‐sensitive strategies to enhance CSR.

title: AccES: A Framework for Predicting Building‐Level Loss of Accessibility to Essential Services Post‐Disasters Based on Publicly Available Information
authors: Zaira Pagan‐Cajigas; Seth Guikema
affiliations: Industrial & Operations Engineering University of Michigan Ann Arbor Michigan USA; Civil & Environmental Engineering University of Michigan Ann Arbor Michigan USA
abstract: ABSTRACT Natural hazards significantly disrupt access to essential services, affecting individuals' capacity to withstand and recover from such events. However, existing hazard resilience models often fail to account for the interdependencies among essential services and lack the spatial resolution needed to assess accessibility loss at the building level. This study introduces the Predicting Loss of Access to Essential Services (AccES) framework—a novel, data‐driven, and people‐centered approach that uses publicly available information to evaluate accessibility following a natural hazard event. The framework integrates open‐source datasets with local stakeholder knowledge to develop spatially explicit models of interconnected infrastructure networks, including power, water, and communication networks, along with their dependent service facilities such as hospitals, childcare centers, and grocery stores. Accessibility loss is assessed by evaluating the disruptions to infrastructure networks and service facilities, estimating (1) the probability that individual buildings lose access to infrastructure services and (2) the expected increase in travel distance to the nearest operational service facility. To demonstrate the framework's utility, a case study was conducted in Cayey, Puerto Rico, simulating the impacts of a Category 2 tropical cyclone. Results highlight spatial disparities in accessibility loss, with rural and socially vulnerable areas facing greater burdens. AccES advances hazard resilience modeling by providing a scalable, equity‐oriented tool to support data‐informed decision‐making for both pre‐disaster planning and post‐disaster response.

title: The stabilizing effect of intelligent manufacturing policy on supply chains: analysis from the new energy vehicle industry
authors: Ruitao Zhao; Zhenbing Yan; Lei Zhao
affiliations: Zhejiang University of Technology School of Management, , ,; Zhengzhou University of Technology and Business School of Business, , ,
abstract: Purpose In the context of global value chain restructuring, intensifying industrial competition, and rapid technological change, the role of intelligent manufacturing in shaping supply chain stability has become an important issue in industrial strategy and operations management. This study aims to investigate whether and how intelligent manufacturing pilot policies enhance supply chain stability under global uncertainties. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on socio-technical systems theory and the perspective of technological sovereignty, this study employs a difference-in-differences model based on data from listed firms in China's A-share new energy vehicle industry from 2010 to 2024 to examine the stabilizing effects of intelligent manufacturing pilots. Findings Intelligent manufacturing pilot policies significantly enhance supply chain stability by reducing supplier volatility and customer volatility. This effect is positively moderated by diversification breakthrough, information flow facilitation, and physical flow optimization. The stabilizing effect is more pronounced among firms with stronger demand for cross-boundary innovation and higher levels of supply-demand uncertainty. Originality/value This study integrates socio-technical systems theory and technological sovereignty, offering new insights into how intelligent technologies reshape supply chain stability amid global value chain restructuring.

title: The Recursive Relationship Between Technology and Regulations: Managing Landscape Frictions in the Financial Services Industry
authors: Ake Freij; Mickael Buffart; Karl Wennberg
affiliations: Stockholm School of Economics
abstract: Firms increasingly rely on information technology (IT) to meet regulatory demands, yet information systems research typically examines organizational responses to individual regulations. This leaves unclear how firms adapt when multiple regulations with fragmented purposes simultaneously govern shared data, technologies, and expertise, and when technologies introduced for compliance themselves become objects of regulation. We investigate this problem through an analysis of 624 documents covering 44 major European Union regulatory frameworks, assisted by topic modelling and a large language model, and 60 interviews with experts and senior practitioners in Nordic financial services. We develop the concept of landscape frictions: structural tensions that emerge from the asymmetry between fragmented regulatory purposes and integrated organizational practice. We identify three such frictions and corresponding responses: purposive fragmentation prompts firms to reconcile operational and strategic data governance; recursive dynamics prompt them to design reversible IT architectures; and categorical ambiguity prompts them to translate logics across functions and organizational boundaries. Each response enables compliance while also generating constraints that sustain or intensify other frictions. The study contributes to IS research by shifting the unit of analysis from the bilateral regulation–firm relationship to the regulatory landscape–firm relationship and by explaining the recursive relationship between regulation and IT as an ongoing process rather than a succession of discrete compliance events. For managers and policymakers, the findings identify three landscape-level risks: reconciliation, reversibility, and translation risks, that complement conventional assessments of regulatory and technological risk.

title: Within‐Sector Job Mobility and Worker Outcomes in England's Adult Social Care Sector
authors: Akbar Ullah; William Whittaker; Carol Woodhams; Carol Atkinson
affiliations: Health Organisation, Policy and Economics (HOPE) The University of Manchester Manchester UK; NIHR Applied Research Collaboration Greater Manchester The University of Manchester Manchester UK; Institute of Population Health University of Liverpool Liverpool UK; Surrey Business School University of Surrey Guildford UK; Centre for Decent Work and Productivity Manchester Metropolitan University Manchester UK
abstract: ABSTRACT England's adult social care sector faces persistently high staff turnover. This article examines the effects of individual‐level within‐sector job mobility on hourly pay and working hours and identifies the employer types and contractual arrangements that attract such mobility. Using an event‐study difference‐in‐differences (DiD) design, we show that job mobility increases hourly pay by 4.5% in the first year, rising to 6.1% after 5 years. Instrumental variable analyses either corroborate the DiD estimates or show higher impacts. Mobility also raises weekly working hours and reduces the likelihood of 0‐h contracts by around 7.0 percentage points. Employer‐specific wage premia account for nearly half of observed pay gains, whereas worker–employer match effects play little role. Workers predominantly move to higher paying employers—particularly local authorities and community‐based services—into fixed‐hours contracts and out of direct care roles. Moves into 0‐h contracts result in modest pay losses. Men experience larger pay gains from mobility than women.

title: Revitalizing Leadership Research: Three Directions
authors: Corinne Post
affiliations: Villanova University
abstract: Abstract The contributions in this Point‐Counterpoint present divergent directions for revitalizing research on leadership. All three pieces express concerns with the current state of behavioral leadership research but place varying weight on those problems. How the three contributions define the most pressing issues with this literature and how they conceive of leadership itself leads to distinct agendas for the future of leadership studies: leadership as relationships in action, a theory‐based view of leadership, and a many‐valued logic approach. The introduction to this collection summarizes these perspectives, highlights where they converge and diverge, and considers their implications for the future of leadership scholarship. It concludes that leadership research is unlikely to advance by converging on a single paradigm. Rather, advances will more likely come from dialogue and debate, just like that occurring among the contributions to this Point‐Counterpoint.

Does Gender Matter? Gender Signals in a UK Equity Crowdfunding Experiment
authors: Federica Alberti; Xing Huang; Karen Johnston
affiliations: University of Portsmouth Faculty of Business and Law Richmond Building, Portland St Portsmouth PO1 3DE UK; University of Reading, Henley Business School University of Reading Reading RG6 6UD UK
abstract: Abstract While research shows that women entrepreneurs often struggle to secure funding from traditional loan institutions, crowdfunding offers a unique channel to bypass traditional loan gatekeepers and directly access funds from the public. This study explores whether the gender of the entrepreneur sends a signal to a funder, specifically, whether gender homophily affects the organisational attractiveness of a business venture. Additionally, we explore if there are any effects of the organization type and equity return. Using an online survey experiment with UK participants ( n = 4510), via Prolific, we manipulated the gender of the entrepreneur (woman vs. man), the organization type (healthcare vs. fintech) and the equity return (5% vs. 10%) for a hypothetical business venture. Our findings may help explain the mixed results of extant research on gender and entrepreneurship. We found that the organization type, equity returns and experience of funders play a role in the extent to which funders find an organization attractive and willingness to support a business venture. Specifically, our findings show that healthcare ventures were more attractive to women, while men were more attracted to greater equity returns. As a scholarly contribution, we suggest that gender value homophily may partly explain the nuanced findings.

title: Navigating the Digital Capital Paradox: Whether and How It Impacts Export Intensity
authors: Yuge Dong; Xinming He; Markus Blut
affiliations: Shanghai Business School 2271 West Zhong Shan Rd. Shanghai 200235 China; Durham University Business School Durham University Durham DH1 1SL UK
abstract: Abstract Established firms are making substantial investments in digital capital (DC) – that is, capitalized software and systems – to enhance exports, yet they often face perplexing, even negative returns. We argue that this tension reflects an inherent resource–liability paradox, where DC acts simultaneously as a strategic resource and an operational liability. Drawing on paradox theory, we examine a framework that specifies how dynamic capability and external institutional frictions shape the outcomes of this persistent tension. Using longitudinal data of Chinese listed firms, we find that the unmanaged paradox manifests as a significant negative impact on export intensity. We theorize and demonstrate that a strong firm‐level digital orientation (DO) enables firms to reconcile the tension and reverse the negative effect. Informal institutional distance exacerbates the core paradox, while formal distance does not, highlighting the primacy of implicit, cognitive frictions over explicit, regulatory costs. Our study enriches the export literature and paradox theory by identifying DO as a higher level dynamic capability and advancing understanding of contextual intensification by disentangling the distinct roles of formal and informal institutional distances. Hence, realizing DC's international value depends not on the investment itself, but on the firm's ability to manage these internal contradictions within challenging institutional contexts.

title: China's Initial Public Offering Peer‐based Valuation: Market versus Regulatory Pricing Regimes
authors: Wei Zhang; Xiong Xiong; Guanying Wang; Nianhang Xu
affiliations: School of Finance Tianjin University of Finance and Economics Tianjin China; Laboratory of Computation and Analytics of Complex Management Systems (CACMS) Tianjin University Tianjin China; College of Management and Economics Tianjin University Tianjin China; School of Business Renmin University of China Beijing China
abstract: Abstract In 2014, China's initial public offering (IPO) valuation regime shifted from market‐based pricing to a regulatory system with a de facto 23× P/E ratio cap. This institutional change provides a compelling setting to examine how institutional constraints affect valuation efficiency and information transmission. Using a sample of IPOs and hand‐collected peer firms, we document that regulated IPOs are systematically undervalued by 42–56.9% relative to their peers. Their valuations negatively predict post‐IPO returns, while market‐priced IPOs exhibit no such pattern. A low‐minus‐high price‐to‐value strategy yields annualized abnormal returns of 15.6% for IPOs under regulatory pricing, with no comparable profits under market pricing. These effects appear to operate through two interconnected channels: corporate competitiveness and stock price informativeness. Rather than reflecting costly signalling, constrained valuation serves as an information revelation mechanism of firm quality. Our findings provide novel evidence on how institutional frictions shape information transmission beyond conventional signalling incentives.

title: How ventures maintain stakeholder support amidst operational legitimacy threats
authors: Alex Murray; Susan Cohen; Farhan Iqbal
affiliations: Department of Management Lundquist College of Business, University of Oregon Eugene Oregon USA; Department of Management Terry College of Business, University of Georgia Athens Georgia USA; Department of Management and Entrepreneurship Kelley School of Business, Indiana University Bloomington Indiana USA
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We explore how ventures mitigate operational legitimacy threats— threats that originate within the venture and challenge claims relating to the venture's ability to deliver on its promised value proposition . Through an inductive study of four ventures working to deliver their promised products following successful crowdfunding campaigns, we reveal a process of three rhetorical practices that ventures can use to maintain stakeholder support: humanizing the venture , normalizing setbacks and resolutions , and revising pragmatic claims . The first two practices contribute to the formation of dispositional legitimacy buffers that allow the third practice to be effective in mitigating fallout from exposed operational legitimacy threats. We conclude by offering contributions to the cultural entrepreneurship literature and to research on venture–stakeholder communication. Managerial Summary Entrepreneurs must often determine whether to disclose operational issues to stakeholders. On one hand, entrepreneurs may resolve these operational issues without stakeholders ever knowing of their occurrence. On the other hand, such issues could balloon to negatively impact whether a venture can deliver its promised offering. We identify three rhetorical practices, two of which entrepreneurs can utilize before an operational issue even occurs, to generate favorable judgments with stakeholders and increase the likelihood that their ventures will be able to maintain support if an operational issue becomes exposed.

title: Correction to: You Cannot Force Me Into Caregiving: Paternity Leave and the Child Penalty
AVERAGE TREATMENT EFFECT LOCALIZATION: PROJECTION METHODS IN SYNTHETIC CONTROL
authors: Ruei-Chi Lee
affiliations: Rutgers University
abstract: Many real-world policies and business interventions require assessing short-term effects to inform timely decisions, even though most causal inference methods focus on long-term average treatment effects. In this article, we introduce average treatment effect localization (ATEL), which captures localized, short-term policy impacts in panel data settings with a single treated unit and provides early indicators of policy impact. To accommodate both time-varying and nonlinear effects of observed and unobserved covariates, we propose a nonparametric model for untreated outcome, interpreted as a time-varying factor model via sieve approximation. Estimating the time-varying factor model is challenging due to the boundary bias and identification. Our estimation method based on diversified projection can effectively address these issues. We develop an asymptotic distribution theory to facilitate inference for the ATEL estimator. In an empirical application, we apply our proposed methodology to assess the impact of right-to-carry laws on violent crime rate.

title: Seigneurial institutions and Holland's seventeenth‐century miracle
authors: Frederik Buylaert; Thijs Lambrecht; Jim van der Meulen; Rombert Stapel; Arie van Steensel; Maarten J. Prins; Kaat Cappelle; Niels Fieremans
affiliations: Ghent University Ghent Belgium; ING Huyghens Amsterdam the Netherlands; International Institute of Social History Amsterdam the Netherlands; Groningen University Groningen the Netherlands
abstract: Abstract This article revisits the claim that Holland owed much of its seventeenth‐century efflorescence to the absence of feudal constraints on its economy. Because Holland was relatively late to develop in the eleventh and twelfth centuries, it supposedly missed the European Feudal Revolution, thus opening space for an exceptional long‐run development. Whilst this view is correct for serfdom and landlordship, it is not for seigneurial lordship, another constituent of feudalism as a controversial concept. A survey reveals that seigneuries were not rarer than in other Netherlandish principalities. Seigneurial surplus‐extraction, which might have stifled economic innovation, was low, but this too was not unique to Holland. Rather than being a stumbling block for dynamism, however, seigneuries supported economic change. Apart from shielding burgeoning rural proto‐industries from urban rent‐seeking, seigneurial regulations put in place a framework for the rise of factor markets for land and labour. There is truth to the claim that the Holland countryside was an open society that prospered thanks to secure property rights and the agency for villagers to pursue a wide range of strategies, but Holland did not have these advantages because it was free of lordship. In fact, seigneuries were part of its exceptional political economy.

title: Metric capital: how academic indicators become interactional resource
authors: Łukasz Remisiewicz
abstract: Abstract This article develops a sociological theory of how academic indicators acquire force in academic life. Based on Randall Collins’s interaction ritual theory, it distinguishes three analytically separate layers that are often conflated in studies of bibliometrics: reception traces, valuation tokens, and metric capital. Academic interactions leave traces in the form of citations, mentions, and article downloads. Selected ones are then stabilized by digital infrastructures, which reduce them to tokens by collecting, certifying, and making them internally comparable. Individual academics accumulate these tokens into a portfolio of objectified symbols that can be mobilized in further interactions—both informally and formally. In this way, they constitute a form of capital. It is activated through three mechanisms. First, it influences the course of interaction before it begins (pre-entrainment), is transferable through structural holes, and also allows for the closure of discussions during evaluation rituals where diverse evaluation cultures or low competence in assessing the quality of work exist. Metric capital can be separated from a scientist’s informal reputation within the scientific community in various ways. The article thus proposes to expand the discussion about measures from the question of what they represent to the question of how they interactively shape the scientific order.

title: Moving towards decolonizing health professions education research: an analysis of global network patterns and equity implications
authors: Peerasit Sitthirat; Seksan Yoadsanit; Phuphinyo Limchantra; Kanjaree Suppawittaya; Suttithan Suwannoppakun; Piwat Suppawittaya; Phanuwich Kaewkamjornchai; Somsak Chunharas
abstract: Abstract Colonialism has left a lasting remnant in global academic community, with research contributions and authorship historically concentrated among high-income countries. This imbalance has made decolonization in research a global agenda aimed at rebalancing power relations across the community. Nevertheless, traditional bibliometric tools remain unable to capture such underlying power dynamics. This study proposes leveraging social network analysis (SNA) to examine community architecture and promote inclusivity in health professions education (HPE) research. We analyzed peer-reviewed articles published between 2015 and 2024 in leading HPE journals, extracting country-level co-authorship data from Scopus. SNA metrics, particularly small world coefficient and centrality, were used to assess collaboration structures, integration patterns, and power dynamics, capturing how power is distributed across the network. The analysis revealed an expanding–centralized pattern: although the research community has expanded globally, with more countries contributing, the overall network structure has remained hierarchical. The network’s small-worldness declined, indicating growing concentration of power within the network core, while stable centrality showed that dominant players have remained consistent throughout the decade. Despite an increasing number of nodes suggesting broader participation, power became increasingly centralized rather than distributed toward the periphery, suggesting the global network remains structurally inequitable and epistemic colonization may still persist. Systemic reforms in research infrastructure, nationally and globally, and in journal policies are needed to enable greater inclusivity. SNA offers critical insight into the structural imbalances that must be monitored to guide process toward achieving an equitable global research ecosystem.

title: Targeted Philanthropy: Evidence from M&As
authors: CARA VANSTEENKISTE
abstract: ABSTRACT I show how firms optimize the allocation of charitable funds around investments that require external stakeholder support, such as mergers and acquisitions. Acquirers increase donations to target‐related charities before making a takeover offer, but scale funds back after withdrawing from a deal. Firms redistribute funds from nontakeover‐related areas to target insider–affiliated charities, employee communities, and counties with a regulatory presence. Targeted donations that encourage blockholder reciprocity and employee commitment are associated with better deal performance through decreased merger premiums and lower integration costs. Overall, the results highlight firms’ use of philanthropy to manage stakeholder relations in takeover decisions.

title: When Do Treasuries Earn the Convenience Yield?—A Hedging Perspective
authors: VIRAL V. ACHARYA; TOOMAS LAARITS
abstract: ABSTRACT We document that the convenience yield of U.S. Treasuries exhibits properties consistent with a hedging perspective of safe assets, that is, Treasuries are valued highly if they appreciate with poor aggregate shocks. In particular, the convenience yield tends to be low when the covariance of Treasury returns with the aggregate stock market returns is high. A decomposition of the aggregate stock‐bond covariance into terms corresponding to the convenience yield, the frictionless risk‐free rate, and default risk reveals that the covariance between stock returns and the convenience yield itself drives the effect in a substantive capacity.

title: Flow‐Driven ESG Returns
authors: PHILIPPE VAN DER BECK
abstract: ABSTRACT I show that the recent returns to environmental, social, and governance (ESG) investing are strongly driven by price impact from flows toward ESG portfolios. Using data on trades, I estimate the market's ability to accommodate ESG flows, which is given by the elasticity of substitution between ESG and other stocks. I show that every dollar flowing toward a representative ESG portfolio increases the market value of ESG stocks by $0.8. The growing institutional flows into the ESG portfolio are the main driver of ESG returns and have caused an annual flow‐driven return of 1.9%. In the absence of flows, ESG stocks would not have outperformed the market from 2012 to 2023.

title: The Financial Premium
authors: JENS DICK‐NIELSEN; PETER FELDHÜTTER; DAVID LANDO
abstract: ABSTRACT We show that bonds issued by financial firms have higher spreads than bonds issued by industrial firms with the same rating and maturity, a difference that we refer to as the financial premium. Over the period 1987 to 2020, in the United States, this premium is 43 basis points on average, with the premium higher for lower ratings, higher during financial crises, and increasing in bond beta. We derive a model that explains the financial premium: banks hold diversified portfolios of nonfinancial debt, and bank debt therefore reflects more systematic risk than nonfinancial debt.

title: Feedback and Contagion through Distressed Competition
authors: HUI CHEN; WINSTON WEI DOU; HONGYE GUO; YAN JI
abstract: ABSTRACT Firms tend to compete more aggressively when facing financial distress. This intensified competition reduces profit margins, pushing them further into distress and adversely affecting their industry peers. To study such feedback and contagion effects, we incorporate strategic competition in a dynamic model with long‐term defaultable debt, exploring various peer interactions such as predation and price wars. The feedback effect represents a novel source of financial distress costs associated with leverage, which helps explain the negative profitability‐leverage relation across industries. Owing to the contagion effect, firms' optimal leverage is often excessively high from an industry perspective, undermining the industry's financial stability.

title: Macro‐Economic Uncertainty and Business Cycle Asymmetry
authors: YU‐FAN HUANG; SUI LUO; HUNG‐JEN WANG
abstract: Abstract We propose a modified unobserved‐component model to investigate the link between macro‐economic uncertainty and business cycle asymmetry of the U.S. economy. The degree of skewness of shocks is assumed to vary with macro‐economic uncertainty. We develop an efficient Bayesian Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm. Our estimates suggest that high macro‐economic uncertainty tends to be associated with large and negative shocks to the cyclical (but not the trend) component. Quantitatively, a one‐standard‐deviation increase (decrease) in uncertainty results in an expected output change of −0.15 (0.10) percentage points. Low quantiles of the growth distribution, that is, growth‐at‐risk, are particularly susceptible to changes in uncertainty.
journal: Journal of Money, Credit and Banking

title: The Effect of Global Intangible Low-Taxed Income Tax on U.S. Multinational Companies’ Cross-Border Tangible Investments
authors: Jingjing Huang; Benjamin Osswald; Ryan J. Wilson
affiliations: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign; The University of Iowa
abstract: ABSTRACT The Global Intangible Low-Taxed Income (GILTI) provision, enacted under the 2017 U.S. tax reform, aimed to deter profit shifting by U.S. multinational corporations (MNCs) but has raised concerns about unintended incentives to shift tangible investments abroad. Using an ex ante identification strategy based on public financial statements, we document that an average MNC increases foreign tangible investment by approximately $256.2 million relative to 2017 levels to minimize GILTI tax. Although this finding could raise concerns that firms are reducing domestic tangible investment for foreign expansion, we find no significant decline in domestic tangible investment. Furthermore, we find GILTI firms increase both foreign and domestic innovation, including capital-intensive technologies. The positive domestic innovation spillovers support the intended effect of the U.S. tax reform in boosting domestic economic growth. Our evidence reveals how international tax provisions, though aimed at curbing profit shifting, can simultaneously create unintended incentives. JEL Classifications: M41; H25; H26.

title: Tax-Related Key Audit Matters and Changes in Multinational Income Shifting
authors: Christof Beuselinck; Nathan C. Goldman; Jochen Pierk; Cinthia Valle Ruiz
affiliations: IESEG School of Management; North Carolina State University; Erasmus University Rotterdam; IE Business School–IE University
abstract: ABSTRACT Key audit matters (KAMs) increase the salience of uncertainty surrounding the underlying accounts. We examine KAMs related to uncertain tax positions (UTPs), which highlight potential concerns to external stakeholders about uncertain tax planning activities such as multinational income shifting. Increased scrutiny may reduce the expected benefits of these strategies and discourage firms from pursuing them. Using KAM disclosures in the expanded audit reports, we find that group-level KAM disclosures are associated with a decline in multinational income shifting when the KAMs relate to UTPs. This relation is stronger when firms are financially unconstrained, when the institutional environment features strong tax enforcement, and when KAMs highlight specific risk statements and auditors provide explicit assurance. Overall, our findings reveal a novel and potentially unintended real effect of expanded audit reports: the salience of tax-related KAM disclosures influences multinational tax planning, highlighting broader consequences of this regulatory intervention. Data Availability: Data are available from the public sources cited in the text. JEL Classifications: H25; H26; H40.

title: When Can Clientelism Serve Democratic Ends? A Democratic Theory of Distributive Politics
authors: SAMUEL ELY BAGG; UDIT BHATIA
affiliations: University of South Carolina; King’s College London
abstract: This article employs normative democratic theory to examine a counterintuitive suggestion raised repeatedly by empirical scholars of clientelism: namely, that practices of particularistic exchange might sometimes serve democratic ends. Certainly, most particularistic practices are widely agreed to undermine democracy, on both intrinsic and instrumental grounds. Yet some observers resist blanket condemnation—and in particular, many highlight the redeeming democratic virtues of certain practices that seem to facilitate collective organization among disempowered groups. Drawing on “realist” approaches to democratic theory, we vindicate this basic insight while clarifying its scope conditions. Countervailing power is a crucial democratic priority, and programmatic methods of promoting it sometimes face serious obstacles: as when clientelist practices are deeply entrenched, or incumbents capture the tools of programmatic competition. Under such conditions, we conclude, democracy-seeking leaders may justifiably employ particularistic practices to promote countervailing power—but only if they respect five constraints tethering them strictly to that goal.

title: The Idea of a Counter-Structure: Rethinking Collective Action against Climate Injustice
authors: JONATHAN MASIN-PETERS
affiliations: Harvard University
abstract: This article argues that addressing the structural injustices of climate change requires rethinking collective action. Disruptive and prefigurative politics are often treated as separate collective action repertoires, but I argue that a just energy transition requires that they work in tandem. To capture this interaction, I propose the idea of “counter-structural” collective action, in which disruptive protest creates windows of opportunity that prefigurative alternatives can then fill. Through analysis of two UK climate movements, Transition Towns (TTs) and Camps for Climate Action (CCA), I show how activists reconfigure structural elements to build new, carbon-free social and political forms. The theory of counter-structural action provides a framework for assessing the empirical cases. The cases, in turn, illustrate a broader conception of collective action that better reflects the social theory grounding structural injustice. Together, the theory and cases support the dual aims of climate justice: challenging fossil-fuel path dependence and advancing egalitarianism.

title: Teaching the past, informing the present? School history education and attitudes toward foreign countries
authors: Soyoung Lee; Jeongmin Park
affiliations: Assistant Professor, Department of Political Science Yale University New Haven Connecticut USA; Postdoctoral Prize Fellow, Department of Politics Oxford University Nuffield College Oxford UK
abstract: Abstract How does school history education emphasizing past grievances with other countries impact attitudes toward conflict and cooperation with the countries today? We examine this question using original data from 34 classrooms across 17 high schools in Seoul, South Korea. We first test whether exposure to anti‐Japanese content in school history education negatively impacts students' attitudes toward cooperation with Japan. We then compare how the attitudes of students educated with a more pro‐US textbook differ from those using a more anti‐US one. We find that school history education influenced what historical events students believed as “facts” and their evaluation of historical events. However, the effect on students' historical memories did not by itself automatically translate into corresponding attitudes toward present‐day Japan or the United States. Our findings offer various implications for studies on international rivalries and historical memories, as well as for debates on the political effects of school education.
